extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, private labelers, retailers, trade associations, counsel, and other stakeholders affected by CPSC section 6(b) disclosure rules and FOIA disclosures
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive guidance and proposed regulatory revisions governing how the Consumer Product Safety Commission provides notice, handles confidentiality claims, and decides disclosure under section 6(b) of the Consumer Product Safety Act (including interaction with FOIA and section 15(b) submissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Renotification for updated information
rubrics_metrics.description: Renotification is not necessary for manufacturers and private labelers to provide the Commission, in the course of its proceedings, with new data or arguments regarding information that CPSC disclosed previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission has an ongoing duty under section 6(b)(7) of the CPSA to ensure that any information it discloses is accurate and not misleading. Firms may provide new information without requiring the Commission to renotify the public; the Commission remains responsible for accuracy of subsequent disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunities to review materials before FOIA disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission provides firms with two opportunities to review the materials that CPSC intends to disclose in response to a FOIA request: the 6(b)(1) notice and the 6(b)(2) notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 6(b)(1) notice includes a copy of materials proposed for disclosure with redactions for PII and Exemption 5 information; 6(b)(2) notice includes the final package of materials to be disclosed, incorporating agreed comments and all redactions, plus a copy of the cover letter to the FOIA requester explaining nondisclosures. Firms thus have multiple chances to identify staff errors before public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on controlling further distribution after disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission cannot control further distribution of information it makes public through the section 6(b) process, so attempts by firms to limit subsequent releases of previously disclosed information may be futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if renotification or other controls were allowed, the Commission notes practical limits because once disclosed, the Commission cannot prevent downstream dissemination by third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice when identity is reasonably ascertainable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission will provide advance notice and opportunity to comment if a reasonable person who lacks specialized expertise can readily ascertain the identity of the manufacturer or private labeler from the information proposed to be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule adopts an objective 'reasonable person' standard rather than a subjective sentence that could create inconsistency. If the identity is readily ascertainable under this standard, the Commission will provide section 6(b) notice to the firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic notification procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission authorizes electronic 6(b) notices and directs staff to transmit requisite notices through an electronic medium whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current practice: FOIA Office sends 6(b)(1) and 6(b)(2) notices via secure collaboration software (including copies of requested records, with appropriate redactions). To use the software the FOIA Office needs a current email for the firm's representative; if unavailable, notices go by certified mail. For unilateral disclosures (e.g., press releases), the Commission uses email when possible and other delivery methods when electronic receipt cannot be confirmed. See proposed §1101.21(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period time extensions initiated by firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent a specific request from a manufacturer or private labeler, the Freedom of Information Officer typically has not provided a longer amount of time for a firm to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation deletes the phrase 'Upon his or her own initiative or' to reflect actual practice: firms are expected to request additional time if needed, particularly for voluminous or complex materials. The FOIA Officer may provide different amounts of time upon request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide basis for withholding firm's comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supplemental NPR proposes to require that the manufacturer or private labeler provide the basis for why it suggests its comments should not be disclosed (rather than requiring a strict legal rationale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission expects firms to submit detailed, specific comments, accompanied by documentation where available, because comments assist the Commission's evaluation. This requirement is intended to increase transparency while not chilling submission of useful information; it does not force firms to use legal citation but to explain why disclosure of the comments would be improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission discretion to disclose a firm's comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(b)(1) gives the Commission discretion to include with disclosures 'any comments or other information or a summary thereof' subject to the requirements of the section; the Commission will not disclose comments it determines are inaccurate or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission will assess whether disclosure is fair and reasonably related to CPSA purposes before releasing firm comments. It retains discretion even though the statute requires disclosure on a firm's request; the Commission may also proactively disclose comments when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking information as confidential is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely marking information as confidential is not sufficient to support a confidentiality claim; firms must follow FOIA regulation requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firms should consult 16 CFR 1015.18 (information to provide with a confidentiality request) and 16 CFR 1015.19 (Commission determinations). Revised 16 CFR 1101.24(b) outlines claims of confidentiality. Commission staff will review claims against statutory and regulatory standards before withholding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection (or not) for attorney work-product and attorney/client privileged materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission proposes deleting §1101.33(b)(3) that treated attorney work-product or attorney/client privileged information as generally unfair to disclose; the Commission is concerned firms may mistakenly believe such submissions remain privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission does not expect firms to submit legitimately privileged work-product or attorney/client communications. If firms inadvertently submit such materials, the Commission will treat them in accordance with applicable waiver/inadvertent disclosure authorities. Firms may seek confidential treatment under FOIA regs (16 CFR 1015.18). The Commission will not encourage or promise retention of privilege where a court might later find waiver by voluntary submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other bases for withholding privileged material
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if privilege no longer applies, a firm may contend other statutory/regulatory provisions require confidentiality (e.g., information furnished to facilitate remedial action, section 15(b) identification, trade secrets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a firm may argue nondisclosure under 16 CFR 1101.33(b)(1) (information provided to facilitate remedial action), section 6(b)(5) when identified as section 15(b) material, or section 6(a)(2)/Exemption 4 for trade secret or confidential commercial/financial information. The Commission will consider these claims when determining fairness of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 15(b) submissions and applicability of section 6(b)(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6(b)(5) does not apply to information that is independently obtained or prepared by Commission staff or identified by staff through publicly available sources; information already publicly available is not subject to section 6(b)(5)'s additional protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission relies on legislative history and case law (CPSC v. GTE Sylvania) to interpret that Congress did not intend to withhold information already available to the public. However, information submitted under section 15(b) that a firm maintains as confidential (e.g., test results, supplier names) may still be subject to 6(b)(5) protections where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding confidential business information requires specific identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission will withhold under section 6(a)(2) information that a firm considers trade secret or privileged or confidential commercial or financial information only if the firm requests withholding and specifically identifies the portions to be withheld and the information meets statutory/regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firms must follow 15 U.S.C. 2055(a)(3), 16 CFR 1015.18, 1015.19(a), and revised 1101.24(b) when asserting confidentiality. The Commission will review proposed disclosures, claims, and authorities before making withholding determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary corrective action plans as remedial settlement agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary corrective action plan can constitute a remedial settlement agreement under section 6(b)(5) and thus can trigger the additional layer of protection from disclosure afforded by 6(b)(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and longstanding Commission interpretation treat corrective action plans (ranging from labeling changes to total recalls) as remedial settlement agreements even when not a formal written agreement (e.g., exchange of letters). Even if 6(b)(5) does not apply, firms may still assert protection under other provisions (6(a), 6(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on tactical 'bare bones' submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting only 'bare bones' information to the Commission in connection with section 15(b), while withholding other required information, is prohibited under sections 15, 16, 19, and 27 of the CPSA and corresponding regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission warned that withholding required information could impede investigations; it sees no reason to believe clarifying that corrective action plans are remedial settlements will cause firms to provide less information than required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to file lawsuit to enjoin disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturer or private labeler may bring an action in district court to enjoin disclosure of the document at issue in a section 6(b)(1) notification; a court may enjoin disclosure if the Commission failed to take the reasonable steps established in section 6(b)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This right is expressly authorized by 15 U.S.C. 2055(b)(3)(A). The Commission notes it routinely discloses important safety information even when a firm disagrees with disclosure or refuses remedial action, and may publish unilateral press releases after complying with section 6(b) notice and comment requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of retailers among covered firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Retailers are listed among entities that must report under section 15(b); section 6(b)(5)'s additional disclosure limitations apply to information that a retailer identifies as submitted pursuant to section 15(b) and 16 CFR 1115.13, unless an exception applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before determining disclosure, the submitting firm (including a retailer) must specifically identify portions it claims confidential and the Commission will review the information, claims, and authorities (15 U.S.C. 2055(a)(3); 16 CFR 1015.18, 1015.19(a), 1101.24(b)). Retailer reporting (including confidential customer/supplier/sales data) may be protected where statutory/regulatory criteria are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals process for 6(b) determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Commission adopted the 6(b) Regulation in 1983, it delegated to the General Counsel authority to render all decisions concerning release of information subject to section 6(b) when firms have furnished section 6(b) comment, except in certain situations; a decision by the General Counsel is a final agency decision and is not appealable as of right to the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The General Counsel may, however, refer an issue to the Commission for decision under 16 CFR 1101.71(c). Adding another appeals process would delay public information and is not justified by countervailing benefits per the Commission's response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental review categorical exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supplemental NPR falls within the categorical exclusion in 16 CFR 1021.5(c)(1) for Commission actions that normally have 'little or no potential for affecting the human environment', so no environmental assessment or EIS is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with prior 2014 NPR determinations (79 FR 10721), interpretive or procedural rule updates of this nature qualify for the categorical exclusion in the Commission's NEPA regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act: IRFA not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the APA does not require a proposed rule when an agency issues rules of agency procedure and practice, the Commission is not required to prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis (IRFA) under the RFA for this Supplemental NPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supplemental NPR does not propose to establish mandatory requirements or impose significant obligations on small entities (or any other entity), so RFA IRFA obligations do not apply. See 5 U.S.C. 603(a) and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act not implicated
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supplemental NPR does not create information collection requirements and therefore does not implicate the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRA applies to 'collections of information' under 44 U.S.C. 3501-3520. This rule explains procedures for providing firms an opportunity to comment and does not request or require information from firms, so no PRA clearance is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption not applicable under EO 12988
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 26 of the CPSA (preemption of consumer product safety standards) does not apply to this rulemaking because the Supplemental NPR updates interpretive procedures for section 6(b) and does not seek to issue a consumer product safety standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule implements a provision of the CPSA uniquely applicable to the Commission and not enforced by state/local governments; thus Executive Order 12988 preemption considerations are not relevant here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed effective date: interpretive rule exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the APA generally requires an effective date at least 30 days after publication, the APA exempts interpretive rules and statements of policy from that requirement; the Supplemental NPR proposes to make the final rule effective as of the date of its publication in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 5 U.S.C. 553(d) and exemption at 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(2). The proposal treats the final rule as an interpretive rule, subject to immediate effectiveness upon publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for comments procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission requests comments on all aspects of the Supplemental NPR; comments must be submitted in accordance with the instructions in the ADDRESSES section of the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders should follow the procedural instructions provided in the preamble's ADDRESSES section when submitting comments; the Commission solicits input on any aspect of the proposed revisions.
